cues.text: In the year 1310, under Abbot Rupert, a priest celebrated Holy Mass at the Benedictine monastery of St. Georgenberg , near Fiecht in the Tyrolean Inn Valley.
Immediately after consecrating the wine, he was seized by a private doubt as to whether the Blood of Christ was truly present under its outward form.
Blood That Would Not Stay Contained
The wine, tradition holds, answered the doubt directly: it turned visibly to blood and began to boil.

It rose until it overflowed the chalice in full view of the abbot, his community of monks, and the pilgrims gathered for the Mass—a public sign the priest himself could not have staged or concealed even had he wished to.
A Relic Still Fresh After 170 Years
A chronicler recorded in 1480— a century and a half after the event—that the Precious Blood remained "still fresh as if it had come out of a wound."
This claim drew the attention of Bishop Georg von Brixen.
In 1472, he dispatched the abbot of Wilten and two local pastors to investigate the phenomenon directly.
Their inquiry concluded the miracle was genuine and worthy of continued veneration.
A Sign Recalled Against the Reformation
When Lutheran teaching began spreading through Tyrol in the 1590s, Abbot Michael Geisser of St. Georgenberg is recorded as having invoked the Fiecht miracle directly.
He did so in a public sermon at nearby Schwaz, using the relic as evidence for the Real Presence in a debate his own contemporaries described as decisive.
The relic remains preserved today in the reliquary of the Monastery of St. Georgenberg-Fiecht.

Two documentary tablets near the altar still record, in the plain words of the witnessing community, both the original miracle of 1310 and its later role defending the Real Presence three centuries afterward.
A single Mass's private doubt became, across the following generations, a public and repeatedly renewed testimony.
